claim: Chromatin dynamics are mediated by remodeling enzymes and play crucial roles in gene regulation.
source: Chromatin dynamics are mediated by remodeling enzymes and play crucial roles in gene regulation, as established in a paradigmatic model, the Saccharomyces cerevisiae PHO5 promoter.
evidence: This is a general statement about chromatin dynamics supported by established scientific knowledge and the context of the PHO5 promoter as a model system.

claim: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae PHO5 promoter is a paradigmatic model for chromatin dynamics and gene regulation.
source: Chromatin dynamics are mediated by remodeling enzymes and play crucial roles in gene regulation, as established in a paradigmatic model, the Saccharomyces cerevisiae PHO5 promoter.
evidence: The PHO5 promoter is described as an established paradigmatic model system.

claim: Only seven of 68,145 models agreed well with all data.
source: Only seven of 68,145 models agreed well with all data.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the modeling results from the study.

claim: All seven satisfactory models involve sliding.
source: All seven models involve sliding and the known central role of the N-2 nucleosome, but regulate promoter state transitions by modulating just one assembly rather than disassembly process.
evidence: This is a finding from the systematic model analysis.

claim: All seven satisfactory models involve the known central role of the N-2 nucleosome.
source: All seven models involve sliding and the known central role of the N-2 nucleosome, but regulate promoter state transitions by modulating just one assembly rather than disassembly process.
evidence: This is a finding from the systematic model analysis combined with prior knowledge.

claim: All seven satisfactory models regulate promoter state transitions by modulating just one assembly rather than disassembly process.
source: All seven models involve sliding and the known central role of the N-2 nucleosome, but regulate promoter state transitions by modulating just one assembly rather than disassembly process.
evidence: This is a key finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: The finding of assembly regulation challenges common interpretations of previous observations at the PHO5 promoter.
source: This is consistent with but challenges common interpretations of previous observations at the PHO5 promoter and suggests chromatin opening by binding competition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results in the context of existing literature.

claim: The modeling results suggest chromatin opening by binding competition.
source: This is consistent with but challenges common interpretations of previous observations at the PHO5 promoter and suggests chromatin opening by binding competition.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation suggested by the modeling results.

claim: 147 bp of DNA are wrapped around a histone protein octamer in nucleosomes.
source: The most basic layer consists of nucleosomes, where 147 bp of DNA are wrapped around a histone protein octamer (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about nucleosomes, supported by citation.

claim: Nucleosomes occupy most of the genome.
source: Nucleosomes occupy most of the genome and hinder binding of other proteins to DNA, for example transcription factors (Venter et al., 1994; Bell et al., 2011; Lai and Pugh, 2017), replication machinery (Chang et al., 2016), and DNA repair enzymes (Hauer and Gasser, 2017).
evidence: This is a general statement about nucleosome distribution supported by citations.

claim: Nucleosomes hinder binding of transcription factors to DNA.
source: Nucleosomes occupy most of the genome and hinder binding of other proteins to DNA, for example transcription factors (Venter et al., 1994; Bell et al., 2011; Lai and Pugh, 2017), replication machinery (Chang et al., 2016), and DNA repair enzymes (Hauer and Gasser, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations showing nucleosomes obstruct transcription factor binding.

claim: Nucleosomes hinder binding of replication machinery to DNA.
source: Nucleosomes occupy most of the genome and hinder binding of other proteins to DNA, for example transcription factors (Venter et al., 1994; Bell et al., 2011; Lai and Pugh, 2017), replication machinery (Chang et al., 2016), and DNA repair enzymes (Hauer and Gasser, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation showing nucleosomes obstruct replication machinery.

claim: Nucleosomes hinder binding of DNA repair enzymes to DNA.
source: Nucleosomes occupy most of the genome and hinder binding of other proteins to DNA, for example transcription factors (Venter et al., 1994; Bell et al., 2011; Lai and Pugh, 2017), replication machinery (Chang et al., 2016), and DNA repair enzymes (Hauer and Gasser, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation showing nucleosomes obstruct DNA repair enzymes.

claim: Chromatin remodeling enzymes bind to nucleosomes and convert energy from ATP hydrolysis into sliding, ejection, (re-)assembly or restructuring of nucleosomes.
source: Such 'remodelers' bind to nucleosomes and convert the energy from ATP hydrolysis into sliding, ejection, (re-)assembly or restructuring of nucleosomes (Bartholomew, 2014; Zhou et al., 2016; Clapier et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of chromatin remodelers, supported by citations.

claim: Nucleosomes are constantly replaced to varying degrees throughout the genome by remodeling processes.
source: Hence, nucleosomes are not static but are constantly replaced to varying degrees throughout the genome by remodeling processes, for example, in the context of transcription (Dion et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation showing dynamic nucleosome turnover.

claim: Nucleosome occupancy data from MNase digestion followed by sequencing cannot determine absolute nucleosome occupancy.
source: While such data sets provide quite reliable information on population averaged individual nucleosome positions and nucleosome occupancy, they have two disadvantages: First, the nucleosome occupancy in absolute terms, that is, the fraction of molecules where a certain position falls within a nucleosome, cannot be determined as only nucleosomal DNA was scored and non-nucleosomal DNA lost from the analysis (for detailed discussion and genome-wide solution to this question see Oberbeckmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological limitation explained with reference to a solution.

claim: Population-averaged nucleosome occupancy data loses information on interactions or coupling between several nucleosomes along the same DNA molecule.
source: Second, the information on the interactions or coupling between several nucleosomes along the same DNA molecule in genomic regions of interest is lost, that is, the obtained occupancy map corresponds only to the one-particle density.
evidence: This is a methodological limitation of population-averaged measurements.

claim: Single-molecule data for configurations of several adjacent nucleosomes is available for the PHO5 promoter.
source: In this study, we use the PHO5 promoter in Saccharomyces cerevisiae for which, as a unique exception, single-molecule data for configurations of several adjacent nucleosomes is available.
evidence: This describes the unique data available for the PHO5 promoter used in the study.

claim: The PHO5 gene is regulated via the intracellular availability of inorganic phosphate.
source: The PHO5 gene is regulated via the intracellular availability of inorganic phosphate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PHO5 gene regulation.

claim: When phosphate is amply provided, the PHO5 gene is lowly expressed as its promoter region is occupied by four well-positioned nucleosomes numbered N-1 to N-4.
source: If phosphate is amply provided, the PHO5 gene is lowly expressed as its promoter region is occupied by four well-positioned nucleosomes numbered N-1 to N-4 relative to the gene start.
evidence: This describes the repressed state of the PHO5 promoter.

claim: Nucleosome N-1 occupies the core promoter and prevents access of the TATA-box binding protein (TBP) to the TATA-box.
source: N-1 occupies the core promoter and prevents access of the TATA-box binding protein (TBP) to the TATA-box.
evidence: This describes the role of N-1 nucleosome in repression.

claim: Upon phosphate depletion, a signaling cascade leads to Pho4 activation by inhibition of its phosphorylation and by increasing its nuclear localization.
source: Upon phosphate depletion, a signaling cascade leads to Pho4 activation by inhibition of its phosphorylation and by increasing its nuclear localization (O'Neill et al., 1996; Komeili and O'Shea, 1999).
evidence: This describes the signaling mechanism for PHO5 activation, supported by citations.

claim: Pho4 triggers an intricate nucleosome remodeling process involving up to five different nucleosome remodeling enzymes.
source: Pho4 triggers an intricate nucleosome remodeling process involving up to five different nucleosome remodeling enzymes, some with redundant and some with crucial roles (Musladin et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the complexity of PHO5 chromatin remodeling, supported by citation.

claim: PHO5 promoter chromatin remodeling involves histone acetylation, histone chaperones and probably other cofactors.
source: It also involves histone acetylation, histone chaperones and probably other cofactors that in the end lead to more or less complete removal of nucleosomes N-1 to N-5 and transcription of the PHO5 gene (reviewed in Korber and Barbaric, 2014).
evidence: This describes additional factors involved in PHO5 chromatin remodeling, with citation.

claim: PHO5 chromatin remodeling leads to more or less complete removal of nucleosomes N-1 to N-5 and transcription of the PHO5 gene.
source: It also involves histone acetylation, histone chaperones and probably other cofactors that in the end lead to more or less complete removal of nucleosomes N-1 to N-5 and transcription of the PHO5 gene (reviewed in Korber and Barbaric, 2014).
evidence: This describes the outcome of PHO5 chromatin remodeling, with citation.

claim: The PHO5 chromatin transition was historically among the first shown to be a prerequisite and not consequence of transcription initiation.
source: Importantly, this chromatin transition was historically among the first shown to be a prerequisite and not consequence of transcription initiation (Almer and Hörz, 1986; Fascher et al., 1993; Venter et al., 1994).
evidence: This describes the historical significance of PHO5 chromatin studies, supported by citations.

claim: PHO5 chromatin studies strongly argued for the now widely accepted view that chromatin structure constitutes an important level of regulation.
source: Thus, it strongly argued for the now widely accepted view that chromatin structure, positioned nucleosomes in particular, are not just scaffolds for packaging DNA and passive structures during genomic processes, but constitute an important level of regulation.
evidence: This describes the impact of PHO5 studies on understanding chromatin regulation.

claim: Full promoter nucleosome configurations in different states were derived from electron microscopy single-molecule scoring for the PHO5 promoter N-1, N-2 and N-3 positions.
source: Indeed, for the PHO5 promoter this information was derived from an electron microscopy (EM) single-molecule scoring approach, at least for the subsystem of the N-1, N-2 and N-3 positions, in several states (activated, weakly activated, and repressed; Brown et al., 2013) and from single-molecule DNA methylation footprinting (Small et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the experimental data source used in the study, with citations.

claim: The N-1 to N-3 subsystem of PHO5 promoter chromatin faithfully recapitulates the regulation of the full-length promoter.
source: The N-1 to N-3 subsystem of PHO5 promoter chromatin has been validated before to faithfully recapitulate the regulation of the full-length promoter (Fascher et al., 1993).
evidence: This validates the use of the N-1 to N-3 subsystem for modeling, with citation.

claim: The variation in nucleosome configurations at the PHO5 promoter is intrinsically stochastic.
source: As the variation in nucleosome configurations is intrinsically stochastic, that is, is not the result of other stochastic events in the nucleus (Brown and Boeger, 2014), the use of Markov models for promoter nucleosome configuration dynamics is valid.
evidence: This justifies the use of Markov models, supported by citation.

claim: The use of Markov models for promoter nucleosome configuration dynamics is valid.
source: As the variation in nucleosome configurations is intrinsically stochastic, that is, is not the result of other stochastic events in the nucleus (Brown and Boeger, 2014), the use of Markov models for promoter nucleosome configuration dynamics is valid.
evidence: This is a methodological justification based on the stochastic nature of the system.

claim: The study integrated four different experimental data sets: PHO5 promoter nucleosome configuration data, restriction enzyme accessibility experiments in sticky N-3 mutants, and two Flag/Myc-tagged histone exchange dynamics experiments.
source: Specifically, we integrate four different experimental data sets: the PHO5 promoter nucleosome configuration data from Brown et al., 2013 of repressed, weakly activated, and activated cells, data from our own restriction enzyme accessibility experiments of two different 'sticky (=lower accessibility) N-3' mutant promoters, to address the coupling between remodeling of the N-3 and N-2 nucleosome, and two data sets of Flag-/Myc-tagged histone exchange dynamics experiments (Dion et al., 2007; Rufiange et al., 2007) to obtain a time scale.
evidence: This describes the data integration approach of the study.

claim: After systematic analysis of all possible regulated on-off-slide models up to a fixed number of fitted parameters, only very few models were in agreement with all four data sets.
source: After systematic analysis of all possible regulated on-off-slide models up to a fixed number of fitted parameters, we found only very few models in agreement with all four data sets and were able to describe the effective dynamics of nucleosome configurations during chromatin remodeling at the PHO5 promoter in yeast.
evidence: This summarizes the main finding of the systematic modeling approach.

claim: 173 models satisfied the likelihood threshold after stage 1 using only configuration statistics data.
source: At this stage, we found 173 such models, with the top 30 models presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.
evidence: This is a result from the first stage of model selection.

claim: The systematic approach found models with higher likelihood than the Brown et al., 2013 model.
source: This reveals the power of our systematic approach, since we found models with higher likelihood as well as models with one parameter less and not much worse likelihood.
evidence: This is a comparison showing improvement over previous work.

claim: Models without sliding processes were excluded after stage 2.
source: With this fit we also excluded models without sliding processes (Figure 2—figure supplement 6C) as well as models with less than seven fitted parameters (Figure 2—figure supplement 6D).
evidence: This is a result from stage 2 showing sliding is necessary.

claim: In models with R2 below the threshold, sliding from N-3 to N-2 is increased in sticky N-3 mutants.
source: Furthermore, in these models the sliding from N-3 to N-2 is increased and the sliding from N-2 to N-3 decreased by the two sliding prefactors.
evidence: This describes the behavior of sliding parameters for sticky N-3 mutants.

claim: In models with R2 below the threshold, sliding from N-2 to N-3 is decreased in sticky N-3 mutants.
source: Furthermore, in these models the sliding from N-3 to N-2 is increased and the sliding from N-2 to N-3 decreased by the two sliding prefactors.
evidence: This describes the behavior of sliding parameters for sticky N-3 mutants.

claim: All seven satisfactory models had one regulated process and four constitutive processes.
source: All satisfactory models had one regulated process and four constitutive processes (Figure 4).
evidence: This describes a common property of all satisfactory models.

claim: Within the seven satisfactory models, the regulated processes are global assembly (5 models) and assembly at N-2 (2 models).
source: Within the seven satisfactory models, the regulated processes are global assembly, A (5x) and assembly at N-2, A2 (2x) (Figure 4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This describes which processes are regulated in the satisfactory models.

claim: The rates of all regulated assembly processes decrease when going from the repressed over the weakly activated to the activated state.
source: The rates of all regulated assembly processes decrease when going from the repressed over the weakly activated to the activated state.
evidence: This describes the behavior of regulated assembly rates across promoter states.

claim: Every satisfactory model employs the sliding process away from N-2 (S2*).
source: Every satisfactory model employs the sliding process away from N-2 (S2*) and a process that allows sliding from N-3 to N-2 (Figure 4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This describes a common sliding process in all satisfactory models.

claim: Every satisfactory model employs a process that allows sliding from N-3 to N-2.
source: Every satisfactory model employs the sliding process away from N-2 (S2*) and a process that allows sliding from N-3 to N-2 (Figure 4 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This describes a common sliding process in all satisfactory models.

claim: Two satisfactory models (8166 and 27,443) do not use configuration-specific processes.
source: We found two models without configuration-specific processes, models 8166 and 27,443 (Figure 4).
evidence: This shows that configuration-specific processes are not strictly necessary.

claim: Configuration-specific processes are helpful but not needed to achieve agreement with the data.
source: Thus, configuration-specific processes are helpful, but not needed to achieve agreement with the data.
evidence: This is an inference from the existence of satisfactory models without configuration-specific processes.

claim: The ratio of the effective chromatin closing rate over the opening rate was between 2.9 and 3.5 for all satisfactory models.
source: The ratio of the effective chromatin closing rate over the opening rate was between 2.9 and 3.5 for all satisfactory models.
evidence: This is a calculated result comparing opening and closing dynamics.

claim: Assembly-regulated models after stage 1 had a closing/opening ratio ranging from 1.5 to 4.5.
source: Even just after the first fit in stage 1, all investigated assembly-regulated models in agreement with the configurational data had a ratio ranging from 1.5 to 4.5.
evidence: This is a result from stage 1 models supporting assembly regulation.

claim: Disassembly-regulated models after stage 1 had a closing/opening ratio ranging from 0.25 to 0.65.
source: The few disassembly-regulated models after stage 1 had a ratio ranging from 0.25 to 0.65.
evidence: This is a result from stage 1 models arguing against disassembly regulation.

claim: Promoter chromatin closing and repression of PHO5 transcription were experimentally shown to be faster than chromatin opening and transcription activation.
source: This further supports the assembly-regulated models as promoter chromatin closing and repression of PHO5 transcription were experimentally shown to be faster than chromatin opening and transcription activation.
evidence: This is experimental knowledge used to validate model predictions.

claim: After the shift from phosphate-free to phosphate-containing medium, repression of PHO5 transcription was almost complete within 20 min.
source: After the shift from phosphate-free to phosphate-containing medium, repression of PHO5 transcription was almost complete within 20 min (Schermer et al., 2005) and 65% of chromatin closing was achieved within 45 min (Schmid et al., 1992).
evidence: This is experimental data on PHO5 closing kinetics, supported by citation.

claim: 65% of chromatin closing was achieved within 45 min after shift to phosphate-containing medium.
source: After the shift from phosphate-free to phosphate-containing medium, repression of PHO5 transcription was almost complete within 20 min (Schermer et al., 2005) and 65% of chromatin closing was achieved within 45 min (Schmid et al., 1992).
evidence: This is experimental data on PHO5 closing kinetics, supported by citation.

claim: The models predict a probability maximum for configuration 3 after leaving the initial repressed steady state and before arriving in the activated steady state during chromatin opening.
source: Interestingly, our models predict a probability maximum after leaving the initial repressed steady state and before arriving in the activated steady state for configuration three and some models also for configurations 2 and 4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model dynamics shown in the figure.

claim: Regulated on-off-slide models include nucleosome assembly, disassembly and sliding.
source: We present a new approach for modeling nucleosome dynamics at promoters: regulated on-off-slide models. They include nucleosome assembly, disassembly and sliding and enable a combined fit of data for different promoter activation states.
evidence: This describes the components of the new modeling framework.

claim: The hierarchical approach of global, site-specific and configuration-specific processes allowed representation of different network topologies.
source: The hierarchical approach of global, site-specific and configuration-specific processes allowed us to represent different network topologies, that is, switching 'off' reactions by using a very low rate of a non-global process, and continuous variations among network topologies (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This describes the flexibility of the modeling framework.

claim: 68,145 regulated on-off-slide models with up to seven fitted parameters were investigated.
source: We investigated all regulated on-off-slide models with up to seven fitted parameters, establishing an unbiased modeling approach that can provide insight into aspects of nucleosome dynamics that are so far not directly accessible to experiments.
evidence: This describes the scope of the systematic analysis.

claim: Equilibrium models and models without any sliding within the tested class could not simultaneously fit all four data sets.
source: Equilibrium models and models without any sliding within the tested class could not simultaneously fit all four data sets.
evidence: This is a negative result showing what types of models were excluded.

claim: The identification of essential and directional sliding during PHO5 promoter chromatin opening matched expectations based on earlier studies.
source: The identification of essential and directional sliding during PHO5 promoter chromatin opening, the estimated time scales and the central role for the N-2 nucleosome in all seven models matched expectations based on earlier studies.
evidence: This compares the modeling results with prior knowledge.

claim: The selection of only regulated assembly processes was surprising as regulated disassembly would be commonly expected.
source: However, we were surprised that only a regulated assembly process was compatible with the data, but not a regulated disassembly process, as the latter would be commonly expected.
evidence: This expresses surprise at the modeling result compared to expectations.

claim: The common view on promoter chromatin opening is that it is triggered by binding of a factor that locally recruits a chromatin remodeler, which mediates nucleosome removal.
source: At first sight, regulated assembly counters the common view on promoter chromatin opening mechanisms as derived from pioneering studies at the yeast PHO5 (Korber and Barbaric, 2014) or other, like the HO (Cosma et al., 1999) promoter, but also at mammalian promoters like the glucocorticoid-regulated MMTV promoter (Deroo and Archer, 2001; Johnson et al., 2008). According to this view, chromatin opening is triggered by binding of a (transcription) factor that locally recruits, either directly or via histone modifications like acetylation (Hassan et al., 2001), a chromatin remodeler, which in turn mediates nucleosome removal either by sliding and/or by disassembly (Sudarsanam and Winston, 2000; Vignali et al., 2000; Workman, 2006; Becker and Hörz, 2002; Narlikar et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the prevailing model in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The common view of chromatin opening is based on experiments showing physical interactions between transcription factors and remodelers.
source: It is mainly based on (i) experiments showing physical interactions between transcription factors and remodelers (Neely et al., 1999; Yudkovsky et al., 1999; Natarajan et al., 1999) or between remodelers and modified chromatin (Hassan et al., 2001), (ii) on chromatin immunoprecipitation or microscopy data showing transcription factor or histone modifier recruitment to the promoter upon promoter activation (Cosma et al., 1999; Kowenz-Leutz and Leutz, 1999; Barbaric et al., 2003; Dhasarathy and Kladde, 2005; Johnson et al., 2008), and (iii) on in vitro assays demonstrating nucleosome sliding and disassembly activities for chromatin remodelers (Tsukiyama et al., 1994; Lorch et al., 1999; Längst et al., 1999; Hamiche et al., 1999).
evidence: This describes the experimental basis for the common view, with citations.

claim: Remodelers were shown to mediate nucleosome assembly in vitro.
source: Nonetheless, we note that remodelers were equally shown to mediate nucleosome assembly in vitro (Lorch et al., 1999; Haushalter and Kadonaga, 2003) and wonder if the well-documented remodeler recruitment at promoters upon promoter activation may also result in downregulation of nucleosome assembly rather than upregulation of disassembly.
evidence: This cites evidence for remodeler assembly activity.

claim: Binding competition between sequence specific DNA binders and the histone octamer was proposed as a mechanism for nucleosome removal before ATP dependent remodeling enzymes were fully recognized.
source: Before ATP dependent remodeling enzymes and their active nucleosome displacement activities were fully recognized, it was proposed that binding competition between sequence specific DNA binders like transcription factors and the histone octamer, that is, mass action principles, was a major mechanism for nucleosome removal.
evidence: This describes a historical alternative mechanism.

claim: A nucleosome positioned over Gal4 binding sites could be displaced by adding Gal4 in vitro.
source: For example, if a nucleosome was positioned over Gal4 binding sites in the absence of Gal4 it could be displaced by adding Gal4 in vitro (Workman and Kingston, 1992) or inducing Gal4 in vivo (Morse, 1993).
evidence: This is experimental evidence for binding competition, with citations.

claim: Pioneer factors and general regulatory factors were suggested to displace nucleosomes by binding competition.
source: Recently, the class of pioneer factors and general regulatory factors that have important roles in opening chromatin or keeping chromatin open, for example in the context of cellular reprogramming, were also suggested to displace nucleosomes by binding competition (Yan et al., 2018; Donovan et al., 2019; Iwafuchi et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes recent support for binding competition mechanism, with citations.

claim: A PHO5 promoter lacking UASp2 was not induced during phosphate starvation in vivo.
source: Further, a PHO5 promoter lacking UASp2, that is, left only with the constitutively accessible UASp1 in-between N-2 and N-3, was not induced during phosphate starvation in vivo (Ertel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is experimental evidence for the importance of UASp2, with citation.

claim: The coregulated PHO8 promoter was opened without an intranucleosomal UASp.
source: However, early studies dismissed an essential role for binding competition at the PHO5 promoter as (i) the coregulated PHO8 promoter was opened without an intranucleosomal UASp (Barbarić et al., 1992), (ii) even the ΔUASp2 PHO5 promoter mutant could be opened if PHO4 was overexpressed (Ertel et al., 2010) and (iii) even an overexpressed Pho4 version containing a functional DNA-binding but no transactivation domain could not displace N-2 and trigger chromatin opening (Svaren et al., 1994) although just the Gal4 DNA binding domain could displace nucleosomes in other contexts (Workman and Kingston, 1992; Morse, 1993).
evidence: This is evidence against essential binding competition at PHO5, with citation.

claim: The ΔUASp2 PHO5 promoter mutant could be opened if PHO4 was overexpressed.
source: However, early studies dismissed an essential role for binding competition at the PHO5 promoter as (i) the coregulated PHO8 promoter was opened without an intranucleosomal UASp (Barbarić et al., 1992), (ii) even the ΔUASp2 PHO5 promoter mutant could be opened if PHO4 was overexpressed (Ertel et al., 2010) and (iii) even an overexpressed Pho4 version containing a functional DNA-binding but no transactivation domain could not displace N-2 and trigger chromatin opening (Svaren et al., 1994) although just the Gal4 DNA binding domain could displace nucleosomes in other contexts (Workman and Kingston, 1992; Morse, 1993).
evidence: This is evidence against essential binding competition at PHO5, with citation.

claim: An overexpressed Pho4 version containing a functional DNA-binding but no transactivation domain could not displace N-2 and trigger chromatin opening.
source: However, early studies dismissed an essential role for binding competition at the PHO5 promoter as (i) the coregulated PHO8 promoter was opened without an intranucleosomal UASp (Barbarić et al., 1992), (ii) even the ΔUASp2 PHO5 promoter mutant could be opened if PHO4 was overexpressed (Ertel et al., 2010) and (iii) even an overexpressed Pho4 version containing a functional DNA-binding but no transactivation domain could not displace N-2 and trigger chromatin opening (Svaren et al., 1994) although just the Gal4 DNA binding domain could displace nucleosomes in other contexts (Workman and Kingston, 1992; Morse, 1993).
evidence: This is evidence against essential binding competition at PHO5, with citation.

claim: Binding competition at UASp2 in N-2 had a supportive role in PHO5 promoter chromatin remodeling for wild type UASp1 and PHO4 expression levels.
source: However again, binding competition at UASp2 in N-2, while not essential if binding to UASp1 was boosted by increasing its affinity or by PHO4 overexpression, did have a supportive role in PHO5 promoter chromatin remodeling for wild type UASp1 and PHO4 expression levels (Ertel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is evidence for a supportive role of binding competition, with citation.

claim: The downregulation of nucleosome assembly implicated by the models could result from competition between Pho4 binding to the promoter and nucleosome assembly at the promoter.
source: Therefore, we find it plausible that the downregulation of nucleosome assembly implicated by our models could result from the competition between Pho4 binding to the promoter and nucleosome assembly at the promoter.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: Impeding the assembly of N-2 by Pho4 binding at UASp2 could directly correspond to the downregulated N-2 assembly processes in models 27,443 and 27,448.
source: Impeding the assembly of N-2 by Pho4 binding at UASp2 could directly correspond to the downregulated N-2 assembly processes in our models 27,443 and 27,448 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a specific mechanistic interpretation linking models to biology.

claim: Pho4 binding to both UASp2 and UASp1 may correspond to impaired global assembly in the other models.
source: Pho4 binding to both UASp2 and UASp1 may correspond to impaired global assembly in the other models.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation for other models.

claim: The emphasis on regulation of nucleosome assembly rather than disassembly within the models suggests a new perspective on the effective dynamics of chromatin remodeling during promoter opening.
source: The emphasis on regulation of nucleosome assembly rather than disassembly within our models thus suggests a new perspective on the effective dynamics of chromatin remodeling during promoter opening and calls for experimental assessment in future studies.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the broader implications of the findings.

claim: More Flag-/Myc-tagged histone exchange experiments would allow further discrimination between the models.
source: Firstly, to obtain more information about the dynamics within the steady states, more Flag-/Myc-tagged histone exchange experiments would be most helpful. Measured Flag amount ratios between N-3 and N-2 or N-3 and N-1 and more time points for each ratio would allow further discrimination between our models.
evidence: This is a prediction for future experiments.

claim: Six of the seven satisfactory models predict a similar Flag amount between N-3 and N-1.
source: Six of our seven satisfactory models predict a similar Flag amount between N-3 and N-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), while the satisfactory models exhibit very different behavior for the ratio between N-3 and N-2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a prediction from the models shown in the figure.

claim: The satisfactory models exhibit very different behavior for the Flag amount ratio between N-3 and N-2.
source: Six of our seven satisfactory models predict a similar Flag amount between N-3 and N-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), while the satisfactory models exhibit very different behavior for the ratio between N-3 and N-2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a prediction from the models shown in the figure.

claim: The experimentally observed faster closing than opening is consistent with regulation by assembly and inconsistent with regulation by disassembly.
source: We argued that the experimentally observed faster closing than opening is consistent with regulation by assembly and inconsistent with regulation by disassembly (see 'Properties of satisfactory models - Bounds for chromatin opening and closing times').
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing model predictions with experimental observations.

claim: Single molecule long-read sequencing of DNA methylation footprints makes obtaining nucleosome configuration data at different time points much easier than the psoralen-TEM approach.
source: It should be noted that such data are nowadays much easier to obtain than by the psoralen-TEM approach of Brown et al., 2013 due to the recent development of single molecule long-read sequencing of DNA methylation footprints (Shipony et al., 2020; Stergachis et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2020; Oberbeckmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a methodological advance, supported by citations.

claim: The modeling approach allows derivation of which kind of effective dynamics underlie different chromatin states and the transition between states.
source: Indeed, a major outcome of our study is that our approach allows to derive which kind of effective dynamics underlie different chromatin states and the transition between states.
evidence: This describes a key capability of the modeling approach.

claim: Seemingly the same 'open PHO5 promoter' may correspond to different configuration dynamics or was generated along different trajectories.
source: It may well be that seemingly the same 'open PHO5 promoter' as judged by chromatin accessibility in nuclease-based or by chromatin bound factors in chromatin immunoprecipitation assays does correspond to different configuration dynamics or was generated along different trajectories.
evidence: This is a speculation about hidden complexity in chromatin states.

claim: The sticky N-3 mutant strains used in this study are the same as those published by Small et al., 2014.
source: While we obtained and used the same two sticky N-3 mutant strains as published (Small et al., 2014), we did not use their published chromatin data.
evidence: This describes the source of the mutant strains.

claim: The DNA methylation data from Small et al., 2014 seemed less trustworthy because it was not clear if the DNA methylation reactions were saturated.
source: These were generated by an at that time novel single molecule DNA methylase footprinting approach and seemed less trustworthy for the following reasons. First, it was not clear if the DNA methylation reactions were saturated (for a detailed discussion see Oberbeckmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological concern about the Small et al. data.

claim: In the Small et al., 2014 data, accessibility at the N-3 position in wild-type cells was lower in the activated compared to the repressed state, which contradicts chromatin opening upon activation.
source: Second, accessibility at the N-3 position in wild-type cells was lower (7%) in the activated compared to the repressed (28%) state, which is in contrast to chromatin opening upon activation and the data by Brown et al., 2013 with 55% accessibility at N-3 in the activated promoter state.
evidence: This is a contradiction in the Small et al. data compared to other data.

claim: Small et al., 2014 did not detect any case where all three N-1 to N-3 nucleosomes were removed upon activation.
